content.text:
Lighthouses are among the oldest deliberate navigation aids, and their history follows the history of the sea trade they were built to protect. For most of human history, a ship approaching an unfamiliar coast had only its own eyes, a leadsman's sounding line, and whatever it could recall of the shape of the land. A fire on a high point could tell a sailor where a harbor lay, and a tower that stayed lit through the night could tell him where danger lay. The earliest of these structures grew out of practical need, and their designs changed as the technology for making light, and the understanding of how light could be shaped and seen, slowly improved.

The most famous of the ancient lighthouses was the Pharos of Alexandria, built on the island of Pharos at the entrance to the harbor during the reign of Ptolemy II, probably in the early third century BC. Its exact height is disputed, but ancient writers placed it well above a hundred meters, and it was a marvel that later generations counted among the wonders of the world. It was a tall, stepped tower of stone, with a fire kept burning at its top, and its builders seem to have understood that a light placed high would carry farther over water than one placed low. The Pharos stood for more than a thousand years, surviving earthquakes that damaged it repeatedly, until a series of quakes in the medieval period reduced it to ruins. Its name survived in many languages, and in French, Italian, Spanish, and Greek the word for lighthouse still descends from it.

The Romans built lighthouses along their coasts as part of the same system of ports and roads that tied the empire together. Ostia, the port of Rome, had a tower, and there were towers at Boulogne, Dover, and elsewhere along the routes between Gaul and Britain. The most remarkable survivor is the Tower of Hercules at A Coruña in northwestern Spain. Built in the first or second century AD, it is a square stone structure of several stories standing on a rocky headland, and it has been in more or less continuous use ever since. Later restorations, including a neoclassical facing added in the eighteenth century, have changed its outward appearance, but its core is Roman, and it is generally regarded as the oldest lighthouse still operating. Its survival is partly accidental, since many other towers fell to neglect, war, or the sea, but it also reflects the durability that Roman masons built into their work.

After the collapse of Roman authority in the western provinces, the maintenance of coastal lights became patchy. Harbors continued to need guidance, and some communities kept fires or lanterns burning on church towers, cliffs, or headlands. Medieval records mention beacons in England, France, and the Low Countries, often maintained by religious houses or local lords who collected dues from passing ships to pay for the fire and the men who tended it. In Italy and Spain, medieval lights were sometimes built into cathedrals or fortifications. Throughout this period the typical light was an open fire of wood or coal, which was bright enough to see but difficult to protect from wind and rain, and which gave a light that could not easily be told apart from other fires on shore.

The real transformation came in the early modern period, as the rise of Atlantic trade made dangerous coasts more valuable to avoid. In France, the great estuary of the Gironde had long been feared by mariners, and in 1611 a lighthouse was completed on the rock of Cordouan at its mouth, built under the direction of Louis de Foix, an architect working for the French crown. Cordouan is elegant in a way that earlier towers were not. Its tiers are decorated with columns and carvings, and it was intended partly as a symbol of royal authority over the sea. It remained the principal guide to the Gironde for centuries and is still sometimes called the "king of lighthouses." Its construction also showed a growing willingness to build permanent structures on exposed rock in open water, a task that would become one of the great engineering problems of the next two centuries.

The English Channel posed a particular problem in the Eddystone Rocks, a reef some fourteen miles off Plymouth that wrecked many ships. In 1698, Henry Winstanley, a wealthy and eccentric gentleman, completed a wooden lighthouse on the reef, decorated with ornamental features and fitted with a lantern. It was a marvel of ambition, but it was not built to withstand the full fury of Atlantic storms. Winstanley himself was in the tower during the great storm of November 1703, when it was swept away along with him and its other occupants. A replacement was built by John Rudyerd, a silk merchant turned builder, whose tower was a wooden structure shaped to deflect waves, and which lasted until fire destroyed it in 1755.

The next Eddystone tower was designed by John Smeaton, a civil engineer who approached the problem with a scientific method that was unusual for his time. Smeaton studied the properties of different limes and cements, testing how they hardened under water, and he developed a hydraulic lime that could set in the wet conditions of the reef. He also studied the shape of the tower carefully, so that its base was broad and its profile curved in a way that spread the force of the waves. His tower, completed in 1759, was built of interlocking granite blocks, dovetailed and fixed with his cement, and it stood for more than a century. Smeaton's principles influenced the later design of lighthouses throughout the world, and the original lower portion of the tower was eventually moved to Plymouth Hoe in 1882, when the rock beneath it had eroded enough to threaten it. The tower that remains on the reef today is a later structure, but the form that Smeaton established remained the model for offshore lights built on open rock.

Building on such rocks was only part of the challenge. A lighthouse was useless if sailors could not tell it apart from other lights, and the technology of illumination remained crude well into the nineteenth century. Early lamps burned oil or tallow, and their light was weak. Reflectors of polished metal were added to direct more of the light outward, and by the late eighteenth century the Argand lamp, which used a circular wick and a glass chimney to produce a brighter and steadier flame, came into use. These improvements helped, but the most important advance in the history of lighthouse optics came from France.

Augustin-Jean Fresnel, a physicist and engineer working in the 1810s and early 1820s, showed how a lens could be constructed from concentric rings of glass prisms, each ring bending light toward the horizon. The resulting lens could be much thinner and lighter than a solid lens of equal focusing power, and it could gather the light from a lamp and concentrate it into a narrow horizontal beam. The first Fresnel lenses were installed in France in the 1820s, and the Cordouan light received one in 1823. Fresnel lenses were soon adopted across Europe and the rest of the world. Their accuracy and range transformed navigation, and by the middle of the century they were being manufactured in several sizes and orders, each designed for a particular height and distance. Keepers had to clean and maintain these lenses constantly, and the rotating mechanisms that turned them required clockwork or, later, electric motors. Lights could also be given distinctive patterns, such as flashes at fixed intervals, so that a mariner could identify a particular lighthouse from its signal even at night.

The nineteenth century also saw lighthouses spread into new parts of the world, often in close connection with imperial expansion and the growth of steam shipping. Robert Stevenson, a member of the Scottish family of engineers that built many of the lights around the British coast, designed the Bell Rock lighthouse off the Angus coast, completed in 1810 on a reef that is submerged at high tide. Work on it was conducted under enormous difficulty, with workers living in a floating barracks and landing on the rock only during short windows of calm weather. In the United States, the first federal lighthouse was Boston Light, which had been built in 1716 and was destroyed by the British during the Revolutionary War before being rebuilt in 1783. The Portland Head Light in Maine, completed in 1791, was one of the early federal projects of the new republic, which saw navigation aids as essential to commerce.

In the twentieth century, lighthouses gradually lost their old importance as electronic navigation spread. Radio beacons, radar, and later satellite positioning allowed ships to fix their location without relying on the sight of a light. Many lighthouses were automated, their lamps switched on and off by timers and sensors, and their keepers withdrawn. Automation was often controversial among the men and women who had lived in these towers and carried out their routines of cleaning, recording weather, and sounding fog signals, and many lighthouses that had once been staffed around the clock were abandoned or handed to preservation groups. In the United Kingdom, the last lighthouses with resident keepers were automated in the late twentieth century, and similar changes took place across North America and Europe.

Today, most working lighthouses are minimal structures with solar-powered lamps and automatic monitoring, while the great towers are preserved as museums, tourist sites, and landmarks. Their role has shifted from essential guide to cultural memory, though a light on a dangerous coast still serves its original purpose for ships that depend on it. The long story of the lighthouse runs from the Pharos's fire to Fresnel's prisms and from Smeaton's granite to today's automated beacons, and it is a story of people repeatedly deciding that the dangers of the sea were worth confronting with something as simple as a light.
